title: Prediction of Customer Churn Behavior in the Telecommunication Industry Using Machine Learning Models
harvard_reference: Chang, V., Hall, K., Xu, Q.A., Amao, F.O., Ganatra, M.A. and Benson, V. (2024) 'Prediction of customer churn behavior in the telecommunication industry using machine learning models', Algorithms, 17(6), article 231. doi:10.3390/a17060231.
abstract_summary: The authors frame churn as the telecom sector's largest annual attrition problem (over 30%) and apply a CRISP-DM workflow to a publicly available Telecom Customer Churn dataset (from Maven Analytics; 7,043 rows, 38 attributes) with a 75/25 train/test split. Five classifiers are compared (Logistic Regression, KNN, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest) using confusion matrices, accuracy, error rate, sensitivity, specificity and ROC-AUC. Random Forest performs best in the body of the paper (Table 3: accuracy 0.8694, AUC 0.95, sensitivity 0.8547, specificity 0.8839), followed by Naive Bayes (AUC 0.88), Logistic Regression (AUC 0.84), KNN (0.81) and Decision Tree (0.80). LIME is used for local explanations of two individual customers and SHAP summary plots for global feature importance of the Random Forest; the SHAP top five are Contract, Number of Referrals, Tenure in Months, Monthly Charge and Online Security. The paper positions 'explainable ensemble learning' as a way for CRM decision-makers to trust and act on churn predictions. Note: the abstract's headline numbers (91.66% accuracy, 82.2% precision, 81.8% recall) do not correspond to the study's own reported results.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Only the first half is supported. Section 4.2 and Table 3 (Section 4.3): Random Forest had the highest AUC-ROC of 0.95, 'followed closely by Naive Bayes, with a score of 0.88'; Logistic Regression scored 0.84, KNN 0.81, Decision Tree 0.80 (Figure 6 ROC curves). So RF does achieve the top AUC. However, the paper contradicts the 'often close to logistic regression' part: the RF-LR gap is 11 AUC points (0.95 vs 0.84) and the authors describe LR and Naive Bayes as only 'moderate' performers. No gradient boosting model is implemented (Section 3.3 lists LR, RF, Naive Bayes, KNN and Decision Tree only, despite the abstract mentioning 'Boosted Trees'). Cite this paper for RF obtaining the top AUC, or as a counterexample where LR is clearly behind, not for LR being competitive.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.4.2 (SHAP) and Figure 9 (SHAP summary plot for the Random Forest classifier): 'Contract', 'Number of Referrals', 'Tenure in Months', 'Monthly Charge', and 'Online Security' are the five factors that make the most contribution to the prediction outcomes. Section 4.4.1 (LIME, Figure 8) also lists 'Contract' as the most significant factor for the first customer and 'Monthly Charge' among the top five for the second customer, with increases in 'Payment Method' and 'Monthly Charge' raising churn likelihood. Caveat: the SHAP section's direction statements (that high Contract, Tenure in Months and Online Security values increase churn probability while low Monthly Charge increases it) are inconsistent with the LIME section and with the usual domain findings, so cite the feature ranking rather than the stated directions.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper's evaluation is limited to confusion-matrix counts, accuracy, error rate, sensitivity, specificity and AUC-ROC at the default decision threshold (Sections 3.4, 4.2, 4.3, Table 3). There is no cost-sensitive, profit-based (e.g. EMP), lift/TDL or threshold-tuning analysis of its own, and the model choice (Random Forest) is made purely on accuracy and AUC. The nearest statements are qualitative: Section 4.2 notes the Decision Tree's high false-positive count means telecom companies 'may want to carefully assess the accuracy of the algorithm's positive predictions before taking any retention action', and Sections 1, 5.2 and 6 repeat the generic claim that acquisition costs 5-10 times (or 'eight times') retention. Only the literature review (Section 2.3) mentions AUC and TDL(10%) results from De Caigny et al. (2018).

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment.
claims_supported.where: (a) Dataset: Section 3.2 states the data is the 'Telecom CUSTOMER Churn dataset from the Maven Analytics website platform', 7,043 rows and 38 attributes (a richer derivative of the IBM Telco data with features such as Number of Referrals, Avg Monthly GB Download, Total Refunds), so results are not directly comparable with the 21-column Kaggle Telco file. (b) Reporting inconsistencies useful for a critical discussion: the abstract's 'Random Forest ... 91.66% predictive accuracy, 82.2% precision, and 81.8% recall' and the conclusion's 'accuracy of around 90%' do not match the paper's own Table 3 (RF accuracy 0.8694); precision and recall are not among the metrics the paper defines or reports; the 91.66% figure is the Random Forest accuracy the paper attributes to Mishra and Reddy's earlier study and the 81.8%/82.2% figures are those attributed to Lalwani et al.'s CatBoost model in Section 2.3. (c) Imbalance handling is undocumented and internally inconsistent: Section 3.2 mentions a '2:1 (non-churner: churner)' ratio 'based on Wei and Chiu' and says no rows were deleted from the 7,043; Section 4.1 (Figure 3) says the data is 'unbalanced, with almost twice as many churning samples than not churning samples'; Table 2 reports n = 4,601; and the confusion matrix in Figure 5 (RF: TP 670, FN 88, TN 641, FP 109) implies a near 50/50 test set of 1,508 customers. No SMOTE, class weighting or resampling method is described. (d) Model behaviour (Section 4.2): KNN was the worst performer (specificity 0.5805, 318 false negatives); the Decision Tree had the second-highest true positives (614) but the highest false positives (157) and lowest true negatives (593), which the authors say could lead to wasted retention spend; Naive Bayes and LR performed similarly. (e) XAI method critique (Section 3.5): the authors state that LIME 'only predicts how the present prediction will change in response to minute changes in the input values' and 'acts more like a sensitivity study' rather than explaining why a prediction was made, which motivates adding SHAP for global importance; Section 4.4 reports LIME and SHAP explanations as consistent. (f) Section 2.4 motivates XAI with GDPR's requirement for meaningful information about automated decision logic. (g) No calibration, uplift modelling (only cited via De Caigny et al. 2021 in Section 2.2), survival analysis, fairness assessment, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning or deployment evaluation is performed, although 'deploy a cost-effective system' is stated as an aim in Section 3. (h) Limitations (Section 5.3): no access to billing/credit information and a stated lack of demographic data, which sits oddly with Table 2 including Age and Number of Dependents.

caveats: Do not quote the abstract's 91.66% / 82.2% / 81.8% figures as this study's results; they match numbers the paper attributes to prior work in Section 2.3. No boosting model is actually implemented. The dataset is the Maven Analytics telecom churn dataset (7,043 rows, 38 attributes), a variant of the IBM Telco data, not the Kaggle 21-column file. Sample size (7,043 vs 4,601), class balance and split descriptions are internally inconsistent, and no imbalance-handling method is documented. SHAP direction statements conflict with the LIME section; cite the feature ranking only.
